text_blocks.snippet: Treatment options for high blood pressure (hypertension) include lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and medical procedures. The standard blood pressure treatment goal for most adults is less than 130/80 mm Hg.
snippet_highlighted_words: lifestyle changes, prescription medications, and medical procedures

text_blocks.snippet: Adopting heart-healthy habits can lower blood pressure or reduce the number of medications needed:

list.snippet: DASH Eating Plan: Focus on a diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and low-fat dairy while cutting back on sodium (salt).
Physical Activity: Engage in regular aerobic exercise, such as brisk walking, cycling, or swimming.
Weight Management: Achieve and maintain a healthy body weight.
Limit Alcohol and Quit Smoking: Reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption and stop using tobacco products, which constrict blood vessels.
Quality Sleep: Aim for at least seven hours of sleep per night and manage daily stress.

text_blocks.snippet: When lifestyle changes are not enough—or immediately upon diagnosis if you have high cardiovascular risk, diabetes, or chronic kidney disease—doctors may prescribe one or more drugs. The primary classes of blood pressure medications include:

list.snippet: ACE Inhibitors (Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme Inhibitors): Relax blood vessels to improve blood flow (e.g., lisinopril, ramipril).
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the action of chemicals that narrow blood vessels (e.g., losartan, valsartan).
Calcium Channel Blockers (CCBs): Prevent calcium from entering heart and blood vessel muscle cells, allowing vessels to relax (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem).
Diuretics ("Water Pills"): Help the kidneys remove excess sodium and water from the body, lowering fluid volume (e.g., thiazides like hydrochlorothiazide).
Beta-Blockers: Lower heart rate and reduce the force of heart contractions (e.g., metoprolol, carvedilol) — often used if you have co-existing heart conditions.

text_blocks.snippet: Note: More than half of people with hypertension require two or more medications combined—sometimes in a single pill—to reach their target goal.

list.snippet: Renal Denervation: A minimally invasive, FDA-approved procedure that targets nerves in the renal arteries to help lower blood pressure in patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension.

text_blocks.snippet: You can read more about medical classes through the American Heart Association or guidelines via the National Institutes of Health.
